title: Checkpoint: Faith and the Church
objective: After this level you can explain how the Church shaped power, learning and daily life.
summary: Medieval thinkers split Christendom into clergy and rulers, but the Church also held land, armies and learning. A timeline from 1054 to about 1230 ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: medieval thinkers split Christian society into two teams.
cards.body: The clergy on one side, the rulers on the other. This chapter kept asking where the line between them fell, and how often the Church crossed it.

cards.headline: Faith and the Church, in order

events.label: Henry IV waits three days at Canossa
Thomas Becket is murdered at Canterbury
Sacrobosco’s Sphere teaches a round Earth

cards.headline: Two teams, one Church
cards.body: Medieval thinkers pictured Christendom as two groups: the sacerdotium, the clergy, and the imperium, the rulers, with the pope supreme in the first and the emperor in the second. But the Church never stayed in its lane. It owned cities and armies and often tried to steer affairs of state, as Canossa showed. It dominated intellectual life, from convents to universities. And through the parish and the tithe, it reached every household. Power, learning and daily life: one Church, in all three.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How the Church reached every household through the parish, the sacraments and the tithe.
Why popes and kings fought over who installed bishops, and how the deal at Worms split the power.
How pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals rise high and fill with windows.
Why the Eastern and Western churches split, after centuries of drifting apart.

questions.prompt: Faith and the Church: which order of events is right?

options.label: Canossa, the 1054 excommunications, Lateran IV
The 1054 excommunications, Canossa, Lateran IV
Lateran IV, Canossa, the 1054 excommunications
The 1054 excommunications, Lateran IV, Canossa

questions.prompt: Faith and the Church recap: what was the medieval tithe?

options.label: A fee for entering a cathedral
options.rationale: It was owed on income, not entry.

options.label: A tax the pope paid to the emperor
options.rationale: Believers paid it to the Church.

options.label: A yearly pilgrimage to Rome
A tenth of income, given for religious purposes

questions.explanation: The tithe was a tenth of a person’s income, paid in money or produce, to support clergy, churches and the poor.

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the split into clergy and rulers fully describe the medieval Church’s power?

options.label: The Church also owned cities and armies and steered affairs of state
Rulers had no power at all in the Middle Ages
options.rationale: Emperors were supreme among the rulers.

options.label: The clergy never took part in politics
Popes were chosen by the emperors’ armies
options.rationale: The point is the Church’s own reach.

questions.explanation: The Church owned cities and armies, tried to regulate affairs of state and dominated intellectual life.

questions.prompt: Faith and the Church myth check: what did medieval universities teach about the Earth’s shape?

options.label: That it is flat and ringed by ocean
options.rationale: That’s a 19th-century myth about the Middle Ages.

options.label: That its shape could never be known
options.rationale: Sacrobosco argued at length for its shape.

options.label: That it is a sphere
That it is flat except at the edges

questions.explanation: Sacrobosco’s Sphere, the most popular university astronomy text, argued that the Earth is a sphere.

questions.prompt: How did the Concordat of Worms divide bishops between the clergy and the rulers?

options.label: The emperor picked bishops; the pope confirmed them
options.rationale: Bishops were to be freely elected.

options.label: Ring and crosier for the Church; lands from the ruler
Bishops were banned from owning any land
options.rationale: The ruler still invested them with lands.

options.label: The pope handed out lands; the emperor, the ring
options.rationale: It was the other way round.

questions.explanation: At Worms in 1122 the emperor gave up investing with ring and crosier and accepted free election, but kept investing bishops with their lands.
